project.name: liblouis
project.commit_note: Stage 01 reproduced against the staged ARVO workspace checkout at `bd2f5364d74bdc86af7a13fc690138c453c321de` inside `gt-arvo_60723-workspace`. All file and line anchors below refer to that staged vulnerable tree, whose `swapReplace()` body matches the staged `patch.diff` and the saved sanitizer trace.

staged_source_snapshot.description: The saved ARVO container still holds the vulnerable source tree used by Stage 01. Line anchors in this ground truth were resolved directly against that checkout.

classification.classification_note: AddressSanitizer reports `negative-size-param` because malformed swap-rule state makes `l = replacements[k] - 1` negative on the crashing path. The vulnerable `swapReplace()` code checks only the upper destination bound and passes the signed product `l * sizeof(widechar)` directly to `memcpy()`.

bug_description.original: A security vulnerability exists where the size parameter passed to memcpy is not checked for negativity, potentially allowing negative values. This can lead to undefined behavior or security issues if memcpy is called with a negative size parameter.
bug_description.normalized: Stage 01 reproduced `AddressSanitizer: negative-size-param (size=-2)` in `swapReplace()` on the staged 513-byte witness. The libFuzzer harness writes bytes 0..511 to `/tmp/libfuzzer.ctb` and leaves byte 512 as the only translation input byte. In that table file, the second line `swapcd s <ff><ff><ff><ff><ff> 6` is compiled into a named swap rule whose match side expands through `parseChars()` to 15 `widechar` entries (`255,255,255,255,255,255,1,255,255,255,255,255,255,1,1`), with the first parsed `1` at match index 6, while the replacement side compiled by `compileSwapDots()` contains only one length-prefixed replacement group. The third line's `%s` action stores that malformed rule's offset in a multipass context rule. The trailing raw `0xff` input byte is parsed by `_lou_extParseChars()` to widechar `1`; when translation later executes the compiled `pass_swap` action, `swapReplace()` finds that value at match index 6, walks `k` off the one-group replacement array, and then derives `l = replacements[k] - 1`. Because `widechar` is 2 bytes in this build, the saved `size=-2` implies `l == -1` on the crashing path. The fix adds the missing negative-length rejection before the `memcpy()` call.

source.description: First project-side materialization of the attacker-controlled swap rule that later reaches `swapReplace()`. `compileSwap()` tokenizes the staged `swapcd` line's name and match operands from the 512-byte table half of the PoC.
source.value_from: In `gt_results/arvo_60723/poc`, bytes 0..511 are written as `/tmp/libfuzzer.ctb`. The second line of that file is the exact token sequence `swapcd s \xff\xff\xff\xff\xff 6`, so this step reads the swap-rule name `s` and the five raw `0xff` match bytes from attacker-controlled table data.

tainted_value_origin.description: This is where the malformed swap rule becomes persistent table state. The attacker-derived match sequence and replacement sequence are copied into one `TranslationTableRule`, and the later crash follows those stored `charslen`, `dotslen`, and `charsdots` fields.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: For the exact staged witness, step 3 yields `ruleChars.length == 15` and step 5 yields `ruleDots.length == 2`, so this copy stores a rule with fifteen match slots but only one encoded replacement group.

root_cause.description: After `k` has already been walked past the single encoded replacement group, `swapReplace()` derives `l = replacements[k] - 1` and checks only `d > output->maxlength`. The vulnerable code never rejects a negative `l` or negative byte count before `memcpy()`.
root_cause.note: The staged patch resolves this exact obligation by introducing `int length = l * sizeof(*output->chars); if (length < 0) return 0;` immediately before the copy.

sink.description: ASan sink. `memcpy()` receives the negative byte count derived from step 10, and the saved run aborts in `__asan_memcpy` with `negative-size-param (size=-2)`.
sink.note: The saved sanitizer stack is `__asan_memcpy -> swapReplace -> passDoAction -> translateString`, matching this call site exactly.

parser_admitted.description: The staged 512-byte table half is admitted far enough that the compiler is tokenizing a `swapcd` rule line instead of rejecting the file earlier.

evidence_limitations: The staged vulnerable checkout used for line anchors is commit `bd2f5364d74bdc86af7a13fc690138c453c321de`, not the metadata `vulnerable_commit`. The staged tree is still vulnerable and matches the saved `patch.diff` hunk at `swapReplace()`.

`run_flags.json` sets `runtime_disambiguation` to `false`, so no instrumentation was added. The exact five-byte match token's `ruleChars.length == 15` with expansion `255,255,255,255,255,255,1,255,255,255,255,255,255,1,1`, `inputText[0] == 1`, `test == 6`, and `l == -1` were closed statically from the exact staged PoC bytes plus the staged `parseChars()`, `compileSwapDots()`, and `swapReplace()` source.

coarse_trace.summary: The harness splits the 513-byte witness into a 512-byte temporary translation table file and a one-byte translation input string.

The table compiler builds a malformed named `swapcd` rule `s` whose match side expands much longer than its single encoded replacement group, then records `%s` as a `pass_swap` action in a context rule.
The lone trailing raw `0xff` input byte is parsed to widechar `1`, which is later used during translation to select a late match index inside rule `s`.
Translation executes the compiled `pass_swap` action, `swapReplace()` walks `k` off the one-group replacement array, derives a negative `l`, and reaches `memcpy()` with size `-2`.

fine_trace.note: Unscored harness boundary. The first 512 bytes of the staged 513-byte witness become `/tmp/libfuzzer.ctb`, and the final byte is left as the translation input string.

fine_trace.code:
if (!getToken(file, &name, "name operand")) return 0;
if (!getToken(file, &matches, "matches operand")) return 0;
fine_trace.note: Source. While compiling the staged table file, `compileSwap()` reads the `swapcd` rule name `s` and its exact match token of five raw `0xff` bytes from the attacker-controlled second line.

Applying the staged `parseChars()` logic to the exact five-byte token drives it through three outer-loop iterations because invalid continuation bytes reset `in` to `lastIn + 1`; the token expands to 15 `widechar` entries (`255,255,255,255,255,255,1,255,255,255,255,255,255,1,1`). On this exact witness the first value `1` appears at index 6, so the later input character can match well past the only replacement group.

The lone trailing raw `0xff` byte from step 1 is parsed with the same staged `parseChars()` logic. With no continuation bytes available, this exact witness yields a one-character input string whose only element is widechar `1`.

The staged replacement token is the single ASCII byte `6`. `compileSwapDots()` parses that as one dot pattern and stores `dotsDest.length + 1` followed by the dot cell, so the exact witness creates `ruleDots == [2, dot6]`: one encoded replacement group occupying two `widechar`s.

The malformed swap rule becomes persistent table state here. The exact witness stores a rule named `s` whose `charslen` is 15 from step 3 but whose `dotslen` is 2 from step 5, so runtime can match fifteen indices against only one encoded replacement group.

The staged context rule's `%s` action is compiled into `passInstructions` here. `findRuleName()` resolves `%s` to step 6's malformed rule, and the action stream records `pass_swap` plus that exact `ruleOffset` for runtime dispatch.

depends_on.via: rule->opcode == CTO_SwapCc || rule->opcode == CTO_SwapCd || rule->opcode == CTO_SwapDd

fine_trace.note: At translation time the matching context rule reaches its action, and `passDoAction()` dispatches the compiled `pass_swap` opcode to `swapReplace()` using the `ruleOffset` stored in step 7.

Runtime now uses the malformed rule from step 6. `replacements` points at the two-`widechar` encoding from step 5, while the input character from step 4 is widechar `1`, which first appears in step 3's expanded match array at index 6. Therefore `test == 6`, and the very first `k += replacements[k]` uses `replacements[0] == 2`, making `k == 2` and already stepping off the only encoded replacement group.

Root cause. Because this `swapcd` witness follows the non-`CTO_SwapCc` branch, step 9 has already moved `k` beyond the single replacement group before this read. `replacements[k]` therefore comes from adjacent table storage. The saved `size=-2` together with two-byte `widechar` means the crashing path used `replacements[k] == 0`, so `l == -1`. The vulnerable code checks only `d > output->maxlength`; it does not reject negative `l` or a negative byte count before copying.

Sink. Because the `d > output->maxlength` check did not return, the negative `l` from step 10 is multiplied by `sizeof(*output->chars) == 2`, producing the saved `size=-2` and triggering `AddressSanitizer: negative-size-param` in `__asan_memcpy`.

format.name: 513-byte liblouis table-plus-input witness
format.contract: Exactly the staged witness stored at `gt_results/arvo_60723/poc`. The verified trigger semantics are limited to that exact split: bytes 0..511 are written by the harness as `/tmp/libfuzzer.ctb`, whose second line is `swapcd s \xff\xff\xff\xff\xff 6` and whose third line contains the action token `%s`; byte 512 is the only translated input byte and the staged `_lou_extParseChars()` logic parses that exact raw `0xff` to widechar `1`. Those exact parsed values make `swapReplace()` select `test == 6` against a rule that still has only one encoded replacement group, after which the vulnerable code derives `l == -1` and reaches the saved `negative-size-param (size=-2)` at `memcpy()`. The staged evidence does not justify a broader contract beyond this witnessed 512-byte table plus one-byte input split and these exact parsed values.
